paragraphs: R' Shmuel bar Avdoma or Avdomi.

He was a student of R' Mana, as in Shabbat, chapter 19, halakhah 1 [the supplied transcription has פ״ט ה״א]: he needed to perform a circumcision involving (Rav) Shash’ah, described as berih (‘his son’; the attachment is uncertain) (in the Rif the reading is Shishna), and forgot to bring a scalpel (on Friday). He asked Rabbi Mana, who told him: Let it be postponed until tomorrow. He asked Rabbi Yitzchak son of R' Elazar (who was then among the elders of the generation).

Likewise, in Moed Katan, chapter 3, at the end of halakhah 9: his mother died eight days before the festival; he came and asked R' Mana. And in Chagigah, chapter 3, at the end of halakhah 3, and Shevuot, chapter 2, halakhah 4, he said it before R' Mana.
He is mentioned in Berakhot, chapter 7, at the end of halakhah 1, saying: They did not derive the blessing on the Torah from the blessing after food except for a congregation.

Likewise, he is mentioned in Peah, chapter 4, halakhah 1; Terumot, beginning of chapter 9; Challah, chapter 3, at the end of halakhah 1; Nazir, chapter 7, halakhah 3; Avodah Zarah, chapter 3, halakhah 5. And there, chapter 4, halakhah 2 [supplied: chapter 7]: the colleagues inquired before R' Shmuel bar Avdoma.

notes.text: The circumcision anecdote has the name ששעה, with שישנא attributed to the Rif. The precise vocalization and parenthetical Rav remain uncertain.
The checked Guggenheimer text of Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 7:1 spells the name אבדימא; the notice gives אבדומא or אבדומי.

The abbreviated personal title is retained as R' in the heading and first unit; Avdoma and Avdomi remain alternatives, not merged identities. Hyman's initial student-of-Mana claim remains his statement with R' Mana; the later Shabbat question explicitly names Rabbi Mana in the whole saved Guggenheimer scalar, supporting that occurrence only. The supplied Shabbat chapter 9 halakhah 1 (פ״ט ה״א) is retained beside the named digital match at Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 19:1; the old bounded chapter-9 nonmatch does not prove a lost yod or a printing history. The sequence (לרב) ששעה בריה remains unresolved: the digital scalar has Rav Shash’ah and berih, but does not by itself decide whose son was circumcised. Its plural they-forgot is distinguished from Hyman's singular שכח, retained in English. The Rif spelling שישנא and the name's vocalization remain unverified; Friday is the inherited contextual reading of מע״ש, not fresh calendrical proof. The scalar explicitly titles Yitzchak as Rabbi but leaves his father Elazar untitled; Hyman's father-title abbreviation is retained as R', without importing a full title. The elder-of-the-generation parenthesis is Hyman's own statement. The Moed Katan and Chagigah locators mean the ends of halakhot 9 and 3, and the mother's death is eight days before the festival. Both Mana titles in those separate passages remain R'; no Shabbat title is transferred. The Torah-blessing statement preserves not...except and its congregational restriction. The older Berakhot Abdaima-spelling note remains exact but is not a new whole primary verification. Terumot is the beginning of chapter 9, not the old end reading; all other locators remain, and the final R-S is contextually Shmuel with abbreviated title. The colleagues inquire before him, not he before them. No continuation or legal ruling from the longer Shabbat scalar is imported. All historical English and notes, both current notes and the p002 source hold are retained.

The consulted scan of Hyman III, printed p. 1134, has Shabbat chapter 19, halakhah 1 and, in the final Avodah Zarah reference, chapter 4, halakhah 2; the supplied transcription has 9 and 7 respectively. The English now follows those printed numerals while displaying the supplied alternatives. The whole Guggenheimer Shabbat 19:1 paragraph has plural forgetters and interprets the circumcision as that of his son, Rav Shishaa, in its English translation. This is an attributed interpretation of the ambiguous Hebrew attachment, not independent proof of parentage; the present English leaves that attachment open. Hyman’s singular forgot, parenthetical Rav, reported Rif spelling Shishna and elder/student descriptions remain his wording. The exact Rif and the Ravan edition discussed in Guggenheimer’s commentary have not been collated. The mother’s death eight days before the festival and consultation of Mana occur in the whole consulted modern Moed Katan 3:8 paragraph; Hyman prints the end of 3:9. Guggenheimer notes a three-day variant in G, while the translation retains Hyman’s eight. Berakhot 7:1 gives Abdaima and the restriction to public Torah blessing. These local readings do not establish every identity or the other listed citations; the final Avodah Zarah notice has not been independently located here. The earlier notes retain their wording from the preceding review.
